---
title: "About"
description: "Professional profile of Miguel Cosenza Contreras."
---

Miguel Cosenza Contreras is a proteomics data scientist, computational biologist, and statistical programmer based in Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany. He holds a PhD in Biology and develops computational tools and reproducible analytical solutions for multidisciplinary life-science research.

His work centers on connecting biology, statistics, clinical research, informatics, and automation. In multidisciplinary teams, he translates complex scientific questions and shared analytical decisions into workflows for data transformation, quality control, statistical analysis, visualization, and reporting. His experience includes more than eight years of R programming and the analysis of clinically annotated, patient-derived datasets across oncology and cardiovascular research, including cohort comparisons, longitudinal measurements, biomarker-oriented exploration, and multivariate study designs. His multi-omics work integrates proteomics with terminomics, lipidomics or metabolomics, proteogenomics, and clinical variables.

Since April 2024, Miguel has worked as a postdoctoral researcher / bioinformatician in the Laboratory of Protease Degradomics and SFB1381 - Dynamic Organization of Cellular Protein Machineries at the Faculty of Biology, University of Freiburg, with Prof. Dr. Pitter Huesgen. His current work focuses on building and maintaining modular R and Bash pipelines for studying protein interactions and proteolytic activity, including complexome profiling, co-immunoprecipitation assays, blue-native gel mass spectrometry experiments, and shotgun proteomics. These workflows use explicit parameters, standardized inputs, quality-control steps, Git-based development, HPC environments, and reproducible Quarto reporting.

From 2019 to 2024, he was a doctoral researcher in the Laboratory of Translational Proteomics at the Institute of Surgical Pathology, University Medical Center Freiburg, supervised by Prof. Dr. Oliver Schilling. As the group's main bioinformatics-focused scientist, he worked between clinicians, experimental scientists, statisticians, and core-facility users, implementing shared decisions about study design, clinical variables, comparisons, and statistical approaches in R. His doctoral work focused on proteomics data science and multi-omics integration for exploratory insight into disease mechanisms.

A recurring theme across his work is reproducibility: using reusable functions and software, validation checks, transparent project structure, version control, and documented handover to make complex analytical workflows easier to inspect, adapt, and extend.

## Research Themes

::: {.content-grid}
::: {.info-card}
### Protein Complexes
Bioinformatic pipelines for studying protein-protein interactions from shotgun proteomics, complexome profiling, co-immunoprecipitation, and blue-native gel mass spectrometry experiments.
:::

::: {.info-card}
### Proteolytic Processing
Computational analysis of protein termini, cleavage events, proteolytic activity, and degradomics experiments.
:::

::: {.info-card}
### Multi-omics Data Science
Statistical and computational integration of proteomics with terminomics, lipidomics, proteogenomics, and clinical variables.
:::

::: {.info-card}
### Reproducible Analysis
Human-readable R, Bash, Bioconductor, Quarto, and GitHub workflows with structured inputs, validation, version control, and reproducible reporting.
:::

::: {.info-card}
### Clinical Proteomics
Quantitative proteomics and biomarker-oriented analysis in translational disease studies.
:::
:::
